name: HR Engagement Platform
description: Built a cross-department engagement strategy and cross-device design system for a 41K-user platform

items.label: Projects reused the Design system across multiple products
Estimated revenue generated across two phases
Faster production time across design and development

genz.headline: Clients wanted to attract Gen Z talent
body: Without losing the generations already in their workforce. The company needed a digital solution that could speak to a wide persona range, from Gen X to Gen Z, in one coherent product.

personas.headline: We weren't designing for one persona
body: With the help of analysts, we mapped six generic personas, Pioneer, Giver, Striver, Operator, Crafter, and Explorer, onto a two-axis graph plotting seniority (Leadership to Executional) against generation (Veteran to Gen-Z). That let us pin down what each persona actually expected, valued, and how they'd interact with the platform, without needing one specific client's data.

industry.headline: It had to adapt to different industries
body: The concept started from one client's clear feature requests. But shipping it as a single fixed product meant every client got the same features, regardless of what actually fit their culture or industry.

We combined two survey layers to fix that: the persona survey already used to map seniority and generation, plus an OCAI-based employee survey to read each client's actual workplace culture. Together, they let us assemble a package suited to each client's industry and workforce, instead of shipping one generic version.

cultures.headline: People don't quit jobs. They quit cultures
body: Toxic environments, feeling unseen, and feeling stuck were the three reasons that kept coming up. That became the north star: build a platform that makes people feel like they're growing, valued, and included, and turns individual actions into collective belonging.

gamification.headline: We build the engagement layer around gamification
body: Social mechanics like gifting, sharing memories, and referrals needed a system to sustain long-term engagement. I partnered with an Analyst who owned the sales and delivery side, while I owned the technical architecture, keeping every design decision tied to a business lens executives could easily grasp.

pillars.headline: What makes a reward system actually motivating?
body: I use past research in Game Design and built the reward economy around three pillars:
list: Flexibility: reward levels that flex with both the action's weight and the client's culture
Hierarchy: tiers of rarity and privilege
Evolution: rewards distributed over time so they keep their value
body2: Each reward also needed to map to something meaningful in the real world. That shaped five reward classes, from common experience points to extremely rare custom interface skins.

balance.headline: A reward system only works if it's balanced
body: Too much reward kills the sense of accomplishment. Too little kills engagement. As an R&D side project, I built a C/C++ user-journey mapping tool with a heatmap layer to track reward density, social connection, excitement, and friction across the flow, so imbalances could be caught early.

tenure.headline: Should a new hire and a veteran earn the same way?
body: I designed the journey so early individual actions (bookings, purchases) earn basic tokens, while experienced users unlock prestige rewards tied to team-building actions like organizing events or creating clubs.

reframe.headline: Executives didn't want "gamification"
body: The word itself was the problem: it read as gimmicky to decision-makers evaluating a serious HR tool. They wanted something that felt professional.

To answer this, I built a guideline that let each client dial the expression up or down, more playful or more restrained, based on their culture, and reframed the entire concept as a "Reward-Driven System."
The reframe worked, sales finally had a pitch that landed with both executives and clients.

demo.headline: Slides couldn't sell something this abstract
body: The concept was too new for sales to pitch on slides alone, so we go asked to build something they could actually show. I worked with the dev team to code an early, functional prototype with the core mechanics live and testable, and produced a promotional video using AI to bring the pitch to life.

restructure.headline: The initial feature list mixed engagement mechanics with generic app functions
body: A senior consultant handed me the initial feature table, built from benchmarks and client interest. I worked with the Analyst to restructure it, separating gamified mechanics from standard functions so gamification could plug into any generic feature rather than compete with it.

engines.headline: Engagement drives had to by classified for greater flexibility
body: I grouped every engagement mechanic into three engines:
list: Motivation engine: intrinsic drivers like gifts and points
Emotion engine: personalized, "just for you" content
Social engine: collective contribution like photo sharing and public status
body2: This made it far easier to see how each mechanic would affect the system, and to align it with each client's specific problem.

extend.headline: How do you extend a Design System without bloating it?
body: Since we wanted to reuse this solution across clients, every new component had to be reusable, not client-specific. I worked closely with my manager and synced early with development and management to hold the line on scope, protecting the Design System's scalability from client requests that would have compromised it.

deals.headline: The prototypes and demos closed two client deals.
body: One of them already signed for phase two.

list.headline: Confirming what really matters to clients before deepen research
list.challenge: The reward economy and the R&D journey-mapping tool were more sophisticated than what the client actually used: coins redeemed for gifts.
list.outcome: I now confirm what KPI matter to the client's before scoping investment.

list.headline: Pilot-testing the methodology, not just pitching it
list.challenge: The strategy was grounded in strong research and market trends, but shipped without empirical validation.
list.outcome: Going forward, I would pilot-test surveys and processes like this before rolling them out, to confirm they actually work as intended rather than just sound right.

list.headline: Push for a greater cohesive user-journey
list.challenge: Design decisions leaned on leadership preference more than employee validated needs, and features shipped as disconnected pieces gather from benchmark rather than a meaningful journey.
list.outcome: For further instance, I would further exchange with PM and analysts to develop a solid user requirements methodology.
